questions.stem: In Pavlov's research, dogs came to salivate at a sound that had repeatedly been presented just before food. In this experiment, the food was the:
options: neutral response
unconditioned stimulus
conditioned stimulus
conditioned response
questions.explanation: Food produces salivation without any learning, so it is the unconditioned stimulus. The sound only came to produce salivation after pairing, so it became the conditioned stimulus.

questions.stem: A cancer patient who has had several rounds of chemotherapy begins to feel nauseous on entering the clinic's waiting room, before any treatment. In this example, the nausea felt in the waiting room is the:
options: conditioned stimulus
conditioned response
unconditioned response
unconditioned stimulus
questions.explanation: Nausea caused directly by the chemotherapy drugs is the unconditioned response. Nausea triggered by the waiting room, which has been paired with chemotherapy, is a learned or conditioned response. The waiting room itself is the conditioned stimulus.

questions.stem: What is the difference between acquisition and performance in classical conditioning?
options: Acquisition is learning the association; performance is showing the response
Acquisition is showing the response; performance is learning the association
Acquisition happens before extinction; performance happens only after it
Acquisition involves reflexes; performance involves voluntary behaviour only
questions.explanation: Acquisition is the stage in which the association between the conditioned and unconditioned stimuli is learned. Performance is the observable display of the conditioned response, which may not always occur even when the association has been learned.

questions.stem: After extinction, a dog no longer salivates to a tone. A day later the tone is sounded again and the dog salivates weakly. What does this show about extinction?
options: The association was suppressed, not erased, so learning is separate from performance
The association was erased, then relearned overnight through stimulus generalisation
The dog has discriminated between the tone and other sounds in the laboratory
The dog has been negatively reinforced for salivating when the tone sounds
questions.explanation: The reappearance of the conditioned response after a rest is spontaneous recovery. It shows the association was still stored during extinction even though the response was not being performed, so extinction is not the same as unlearning.

questions.stem: In classical conditioning, contiguity refers to:
options: the number of times the two stimuli are paired before learning occurs
the similarity between the conditioned stimulus and other stimuli
the closeness in time between the conditioned and unconditioned stimuli
how reliably the conditioned stimulus predicts the unconditioned stimulus
questions.explanation: Contiguity is about timing: conditioning is most effective when the conditioned stimulus is presented just before the unconditioned stimulus. Reliable prediction of the unconditioned stimulus is contingency, a separate requirement.

questions.stem: A researcher sounds a tone before a puff of air to the eye on every trial, but also gives many air puffs with no tone. Conditioning to the tone is weak. Which principle best explains this?
options: Extinction is occurring because the tone is presented without the air puff
Contingency is low because the tone does not reliably predict the air puff
Contiguity is low because the tone and air puff are too far apart in time
Stimulus generalisation has spread the response to every sound in the room
questions.explanation: The tone is always followed closely by the puff, so contiguity is fine. But the puff also occurs often without the tone, so the tone tells the participant little about what is coming. Weak contingency weakens conditioning. Extinction would need the tone to be given without the puff.

questions.stem: In operant conditioning, contingency means that:
options: the consequence is given immediately after the target behaviour
the consequence is given on a fixed schedule regardless of behaviour
the consequence is given before the behaviour, as a signal
the consequence is given only when the target behaviour occurs
questions.explanation: Contingency means the consequence depends on the behaviour: it follows the behaviour and not otherwise. Immediacy, the consequence following straight after the behaviour, is contiguity.

questions.stem: A teacher praises students for handing in homework, but only gives the praise at the end of each term. The homework rate does not improve. Which principle is most clearly not being met?
options: contingency, because students are praised whether or not they hand in work
preparedness, because homework is not a biologically prepared behaviour
generalisation, because the praise is given in a different classroom
contiguity, because the praise is delayed long after the behaviour
questions.explanation: The praise is still tied to handing in homework, so contingency is present. The problem is the long delay: consequences work best when they follow the behaviour closely in time, which is contiguity.

questions.stem: A child who was bitten by a German shepherd becomes afraid of all large dogs. This is an example of:
options: extinction
stimulus generalisation
stimulus discrimination
spontaneous recovery
questions.explanation: Stimulus generalisation occurs when stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus also produce the conditioned response. Discrimination would be fearing only German shepherds and not other dogs.

questions.stem: A cat runs to the kitchen when it hears the electric can opener, but not when it hears the blender. This shows:
options: stimulus generalisation
spontaneous recovery
response cost
stimulus discrimination
questions.explanation: The cat responds to the stimulus that has been paired with food and not to a similar sound that has not. Responding differently to similar stimuli is stimulus discrimination.

questions.stem: How does extinction occur in classical conditioning?
options: The conditioned stimulus is paired with a second, stronger stimulus
The conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus
The unconditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the conditioned stimulus
The conditioned response is punished each time it occurs after the stimulus
questions.explanation: When the conditioned stimulus keeps occurring without the unconditioned stimulus, it no longer predicts it, and the conditioned response gradually weakens. Punishment is an operant procedure, not the process of classical extinction.

questions.stem: A person becomes ill several hours after eating a new curry and afterwards cannot stand its smell, even though a stomach virus caused the illness. Why is this unusual for classical conditioning?
options: The association formed after one pairing despite a long delay
The association formed only after many pairings with short delays
The illness was a conditioned stimulus rather than unconditioned
The aversion appeared without any unconditioned stimulus at all
questions.explanation: Most conditioning needs repeated pairings close together in time. Taste aversions can form after a single pairing with hours between the food and the illness, which is explained by biological preparedness to link taste with illness.

questions.stem: Biological preparedness helps explain why phobias of snakes and heights are far more common than phobias of electrical sockets. This is because humans:
options: learn all fears equally easily, so it depends on how often they are paired
have unconditioned fear responses to snakes and heights from birth
are predisposed to readily learn fears of things that threatened survival
are more often exposed to snakes and heights than to electrical sockets
questions.explanation: Preparedness proposes that evolution has predisposed us to form some associations, such as fear of ancestral dangers, more easily than others. Electrical sockets are dangerous but recent, so fears of them are rarely learned. Most people are exposed to sockets far more often than snakes.

questions.stem: In systematic desensitisation, the person first learns relaxation and builds a fear hierarchy. What happens next?
options: They work up the hierarchy, pairing each step with relaxation
They face the most feared item immediately until anxiety fades
They are rewarded with money each time they avoid the feared object
They are given an unpleasant stimulus when they show any fear
questions.explanation: The person is exposed to items from least to most feared while staying relaxed, moving up only when the current step causes little anxiety. Facing the most feared item at once is flooding, a different technique.

questions.stem: Why does systematic desensitisation count as an application of classical conditioning?
options: Avoiding the feared stimulus is reinforced so that the fear eventually fades
The client watches a model handle the feared stimulus calmly and imitates them
The client's fear response is punished until it is no longer performed
The feared stimulus becomes associated with relaxation, an incompatible response
questions.explanation: Relaxation cannot occur at the same time as anxiety, so repeatedly pairing the feared stimulus with relaxation replaces the conditioned fear with a calm response. Reinforcing avoidance would maintain the phobia rather than reduce it.

questions.stem: In operant conditioning, reinforcement differs from punishment because reinforcement:
options: is used with animals and punishment is used only with people
increases the likelihood of a behaviour and punishment decreases it
decreases the likelihood of a behaviour and punishment increases it
involves adding a stimulus and punishment always involves removing one
questions.explanation: Any consequence that strengthens a behaviour is reinforcement and any that weakens it is punishment. Both can involve adding or removing a stimulus, which is what positive and negative describe.

questions.stem: A driver puts on a seatbelt to stop the car's loud warning beep. Seatbelt use increases. This is an example of:
options: positive reinforcement
aversive punishment
response cost
negative reinforcement
questions.explanation: Wearing the seatbelt removes an unpleasant stimulus, the beep, and the behaviour increases, so it is negative reinforcement. Negative reinforcement strengthens behaviour; it is not a form of punishment.

questions.stem: A teenager who comes home after curfew loses phone access for the weekend, and stops coming home late. This is an example of:
options: negative reinforcement
positive reinforcement
response cost
aversive punishment
questions.explanation: Taking away something pleasant to reduce a behaviour is response cost. Aversive punishment would add an unpleasant stimulus, such as extra chores. Negative reinforcement increases behaviour, so it does not fit.

questions.stem: A rat presses a lever, which switches off a continuous mild shock. Later, pressing a second lever starts a mild shock. Which pair of terms describes the two consequences in order?
options: negative reinforcement, then aversive punishment
aversive punishment, then negative reinforcement
positive reinforcement, then response cost
response cost, then positive reinforcement
questions.explanation: Removing the shock strengthens pressing the first lever, which is negative reinforcement. Adding a shock after pressing the second lever weakens that behaviour, which is aversive punishment.

questions.stem: Why is reinforcement generally favoured over punishment when trying to change behaviour?
options: Reinforcement works instantly, while punishment always needs a schedule
Reinforcement cannot be overused, while punishment always leads to extinction
Punishment shows what not to do, not what to do, and can cause fear or aggression
Punishment only works on animals and has never changed human behaviour
questions.explanation: Punishment may suppress a behaviour without teaching a desirable alternative, and it can produce fear, anxiety, avoidance of the punisher or aggression. Reinforcement directly strengthens the wanted behaviour.

questions.stem: A factory worker is paid $5 for every 10 shirts sewn. Which schedule of reinforcement is this?
options: fixed interval
variable interval
fixed ratio
variable ratio
questions.explanation: Reinforcement comes after a set number of responses, so it is a fixed ratio schedule. An interval schedule is based on time, not on the number of responses.

questions.stem: A poker machine pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, averaging one win in every 20. Which schedule is this, and what pattern of responding does it typically produce?
options: fixed interval; responding that speeds up near each reward
variable ratio; a high, steady rate that resists extinction
fixed ratio; a high rate with a pause after each reward
variable interval; a slow, steady rate that resists extinction
questions.explanation: Rewards depend on an unpredictable number of responses, which is a variable ratio schedule. Because the next play could always win, it produces high, steady responding that is very hard to extinguish.

questions.stem: Students rarely study at the start of a term but study more and more as a test scheduled every four weeks approaches. This pattern is most like the responding produced by a:
options: variable interval schedule
fixed ratio schedule
variable ratio schedule
fixed interval schedule
questions.explanation: When reinforcement is available after a set time, responding is low just after it and rises as the time approaches, giving a scalloped pattern. Variable schedules produce steadier responding because the timing is unpredictable.

questions.stem: A child was given a sticker for every correct spelling word, then the stickers stopped. A second child received stickers only occasionally and unpredictably, then they stopped. What is most likely?
options: Both children stop at once, because extinction is unaffected by the schedule used
The second child stops sooner, because unpredictable reinforcement is learned more weakly
The second child keeps responding longer, because partial reinforcement resists extinction
The first child keeps responding longer, because continuous reinforcement resists extinction
questions.explanation: Continuous reinforcement produces fast acquisition, but behaviour extinguishes quickly when rewards stop because the change is obvious. After partial, unpredictable reinforcement, a run of unrewarded responses is familiar, so the behaviour persists longer.

questions.stem: An animal trainer wants a dolphin to jump through a hoop. She rewards it first for swimming near the hoop, then for touching it, then for swimming through it. This technique is:
options: response cost
spontaneous recovery
shaping
stimulus generalisation
questions.explanation: Shaping reinforces successive approximations, behaviours that come closer and closer to the target, until the full behaviour is performed. It is used when the target behaviour is unlikely to occur on its own.

questions.stem: A person who has often taken headache tablets and felt the pain ease takes a sugar pill and reports feeling better. How can operant conditioning explain this placebo effect?
options: Pill-taking has been extinguished, so the brain produces relief to compensate for it
Pill-taking has been negatively reinforced by relief, so it now brings an expectation of relief
The pill is an unconditioned stimulus that reflexively produces pain relief in every person
The relief is a punishment for taking the pill, so the person reports less pain
questions.explanation: In the past, taking a tablet removed pain, which negatively reinforced the behaviour and the expectation that it brings relief. Taking any pill now leads the person to feel and report relief. A sugar pill has no reflexive effect, so it is not an unconditioned stimulus.

questions.stem: A psychologist sets up a token economy in which a child earns tokens for completing homework, which can be exchanged for screen time. This is an example of:
options: systematic desensitisation using a hierarchy
observational learning using a role model
behaviour modification using positive reinforcement
behaviour modification using negative reinforcement
questions.explanation: A token economy is a behaviour-modification technique: desired behaviours earn tokens, which act as positive reinforcers because they can be swapped for rewards. Nothing unpleasant is being removed, so it is not negative reinforcement.

questions.stem: Learning through observation differs from operant conditioning because in observational learning:
options: the learner learns only reflex responses that are already present at birth
the learner does not have to perform the behaviour or be reinforced to learn it
the learner must be directly reinforced each time the behaviour is performed
the learner forms an association between two stimuli presented together
questions.explanation: In observational learning a behaviour can be learned simply by watching a model, and may only be performed later. Operant conditioning requires the learner to perform a behaviour and experience its consequences.

questions.stem: A student watches a YouTube video on solving a Rubik's cube. A week later she cannot remember the order of the moves. Which factor of observational learning has failed?
options: retention
attention
reproduction
motivation
questions.explanation: Retention is storing the observed behaviour in memory so it can be recalled later. She paid attention at the time, but did not retain the sequence, so she cannot reproduce it.

questions.stem: A boy watches an expert gymnast perform a backflip. He remembers the steps clearly and wants to copy it, but he lacks the strength and flexibility to do it. Which factor is preventing the behaviour?
options: attention
motivation
reproduction
retention
questions.explanation: Reproduction requires the physical and mental ability to perform what was observed. He attended to, remembered and wants to copy the backflip, but cannot yet do it.

questions.stem: Children watch an adult hit a toy. One group sees the adult praised; another sees the adult scolded. Later both groups are offered a reward to copy the adult, and both copy equally well. What does this show?
options: Both groups learned the behaviour, but the consequences for the model affected their motivation to perform it
Only the praised group learned the behaviour, and the reward taught it to the scolded group
The scolded group learned through negative reinforcement, so it needed a reward to perform
Neither group learned through observation, because both needed a reward to show the behaviour
questions.explanation: Copying equally well once rewarded shows both groups had acquired the behaviour. Seeing the model scolded reduced the motivation to perform it, not the learning. This separation of learning and performance is a key feature of observational learning.

questions.stem: Which role model is a child most likely to imitate?
options: a popular older peer who is similar to the child and is rewarded
an unfamiliar adult from another culture who is punished
a cartoon character the child dislikes who is ignored by others
a much younger child who is unsuccessful at the task
questions.explanation: Models who are similar to the observer, have high status or are liked, and are seen being rewarded are most likely to be imitated. Seeing a model punished reduces imitation.

questions.stem: Single-neuron recordings from people having surgery for epilepsy found some neurons that fired both when the person performed an action and when they watched it. Why is this relevant to observational learning?
options: It shows observational learning occurs only in people with epilepsy
It proves observational learning is a form of classical conditioning
It shows that watching an action produces no activity in motor areas
It suggests mirror neurons give the brain a way to map observed actions onto its own
questions.explanation: Mirror neurons respond both to doing an action and to seeing it done, which may let the brain represent others' actions as if performing them. This offers a possible biological basis for imitation, though the findings came from a small clinical sample.

questions.stem: In Bandura, Ross and Ross's 1961 Bobo doll study, children's aggressive acts were counted by observers behind a one-way mirror. What is the main advantage of these behavioural counts?
options: They give objective, quantitative data without relying on young children's self-reports
They give rich qualitative data on the children's thoughts and feelings
They remove every extraneous variable, so the study has full external validity
They allow children to describe their own aggression accurately and in detail
questions.explanation: Counting specific aggressive acts produces numerical data that independent observers can check, and does not depend on preschool children describing their own behaviour. Behavioural counts do not reveal thoughts or feelings.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a learner characteristic that can influence learning?
options: the learner's prior knowledge of the topic
the number of desks in the classroom
the schedule of the school bus each morning
the colour of the textbook cover
questions.explanation: Characteristics of the learner include prior knowledge, age, motivation, abilities, anxiety and cultural background. Features of the room or materials are environmental factors, not characteristics of the learner.

questions.stem: A psychologist uses cognitive-behavioural therapy with a seven-year-old who is anxious about school. Which change best tailors CBT to this client?
options: replacing all behavioural tasks with long discussions of abstract beliefs
doubling the session length so more adult material can be covered
using simple language, drawings and involving the parents in practice
using the same written worksheets designed for adult clients
questions.explanation: CBT can be adapted to a learner's age, cognitive ability, language and culture. Young children benefit from concrete, visual activities and family involvement rather than abstract discussion.

questions.stem: The Psychology Board of Australia publishes guidelines for psychological research and practice. Their purpose is to protect:
options: only the funding bodies that pay for psychological research
only psychologists from complaints made by research participants
the right of universities to publish any results they obtain
participants, the reputation of psychology and psychologists themselves
questions.explanation: The guidelines protect research participants, the reputation of the profession and psychologists themselves. Protecting participants' wellbeing and rights is central, not just protecting researchers.

questions.stem: In Watson and Rayner's 1920 study, an infant known as Little Albert was conditioned to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise. Which current ethical guideline did the study most clearly contravene?
options: Participants must be told the results before the study begins
Participants must be protected from lasting psychological harm
Participants must be paid for the time they spend in the study
Participants must be over 18 years old to take part in any research
questions.explanation: The study deliberately created a fear in an infant, and no attempt was made to remove it before he left the study. Current guidelines require researchers to protect participants' wellbeing and not cause lasting harm. Children can take part in research with consent from parents or guardians.

questions.stem: In the 1961 Bobo doll study, preschool children watched an adult attack a doll and were then mildly frustrated before being observed. Why would this raise concerns under current guidelines?
options: Observers counted behaviour, which breaches the children's right to privacy
The study used a control group, which denied some children a benefit
Young children were exposed to aggression and distress that may have affected them
The children were rewarded with toys, which is not permitted in research
questions.explanation: Exposing very young children to aggressive models and deliberately frustrating them risked distress and teaching aggression, which conflicts with respect for participants' wellbeing. Using a control group and recording behaviour are standard, acceptable practices.

questions.stem: Seligman and Maier's 1967 study gave dogs inescapable electric shocks; many later failed to escape shock in a shuttle box even when escape was possible. Why would this study be unlikely to gain ethics approval today?
options: It used a control group of dogs that did not receive any shocks at all
It measured behaviour in a shuttle box rather than using a self-report
It caused deliberate pain and distress to animals, which must be minimised and justified
It did not obtain informed consent from each dog before it took part in the study
questions.explanation: Current standards for animal research require pain and distress to be avoided or minimised and justified by the value of the research. Repeated inescapable shock causes severe distress. Animals cannot consent, so the requirement is about welfare rather than consent.
